item.title: Heat waves: Vpod writes to the Council of State
item.description: The union calls for an ad hoc directive and infrastructure investments against the heat in Ticino.

The Vpod union wrote to the State Council of the Canton of Ticino to request an ad hoc directive against heat waves. The request, reported by the Region, aims to avoid that, in the absence of corrective measures, responses to climate emergencies arrive late and improvised.
The Vpod, an acronym that represents public and parapublic personnel, stresses the need to address the problem of extreme temperatures with structural tools. The letter sent to the cantonal executive is not a simple report: it is a formal request for the Canton to provide clear guidelines and targeted investments in infrastructure.
The theme is not new for Ticino, where summers are getting hotter and cities like Lugano, Bellinzona and Locarno suffer from the heat island effect. For those who work outdoors — construction sites, agriculture, road maintenance — extreme heat can make conditions unbearable. An ad hoc directive could introduce clear rules on mandatory breaks, reduced hours and access to water. For those who work in the office, however, the problem is air conditioning: infrastructure investments could improve the insulation of buildings and reduce dependence on air conditioning.

item.title: Los Vencedores: the film about the Falklands seen by the inhabitants
item.description: The director Pablo Aparo presents at Locarno his documentary that tells the conflict of the Falklands from the point of view of the residents of the islands.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Documentary film about the Falklands presented in Locarno - Director Pablo Aparo chooses the point of view of the inhabitants - Screened as part of the Locarno Film Festival - Try to tell the conflict from a local perspective
## Key facts - **What**: Presentation of the documentary 'Los vencedores' - When: During the Locarno Film Festival (dates not specified in the source) - Where: Locarno, Canton of Ticino - Who: Director Pablo Aparo - Amount: not yet specified
In ‘Los vencedores’, Pablo Aparo decides to go and tell the story of the Falklands from the point of view of its inhabitants, perhaps finding the key to a new beginning. The film was presented as part of the culture section of the Locarno Film Festival, as reported by the local source. The director's choice is to shift his gaze from traditional narratives about the Anglo-Argentine conflict towards the voices of those who live daily on the islands. This approach aims to explore not only the political and military consequences of conflict, but also the human, social and cultural experiences of local communities. The projection is part of a context of reflection on collective memories and the possibilities of reconciliation after periods of international tension. The title itself, 'Los vencedores' (the winners), suggests an ironic or critical reflection on the notions of victory and defeat in recent history. Aparo's work is added to a series of productions ## Analysis of the cinematographic context - The Locarno Film Festival regularly hosts sections dedicated to commitment documentaries - The film is part of a global trend of historical reinterpretation from below - The choice of the point of view of the inhabitants is increasingly common in contemporary works
Pablo Aparo's decision to tell the Falklands through the eyes of the residents reflects a methodology that is increasingly widespread in international documentary cinema: starting from local memory to reconstruct events of global scope. This approach allows you to discover details often absent in history books, such as daily routines, perceptions of danger, forms of civil resistance or simply the way in which communities have continued to live despite the conflict. In the case of the Falklands, where the dominant narrative has long been military and diplomatic, giving voice to the inhabitants means highlighting aspects such as adapting to foreign military presence, managing limited resources, or maintaining isolated cultural identities. The film could therefore contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the conflict, not as a simple contrast between two states, but as an experience lived by civilian populations. This type of work is also linked to broader debates on the role of memory in post-conflict, on how societies process collective trauma and on which narratives are privileged over time.

item.description: The VPOD union asks the Council of State for a structured directive to manage heat waves in public offices and schools, inspired by the Geneva model
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - VPED asks for a directive by State and schools - Request sent to the Council of State on 5 August 2026 - Geneva has already adopted a similar directive - Temperature monitoring is necessary in the buildings
## Key facts - **What**: Request to adopt a directive to anticipate, prevent and address periods of heightened heat alert - When: Request formulated after the Government-unions meeting of 5 August 2026 - Where: State and schools of the Canton of Ticino - Who: VPOD Co-Secretary Edoardo Cappelletti, on behalf of the Swiss Union of Public and Social Health Service Personnel (VPOD) - Amount: not yet specified
VPOD Co-Secretary Edoardo Cappelletti wrote to the State Council requesting a more structured and proactive intervention to address the heatwave in the State and in schools, following the meeting between the Government and trade unions on 5 August 2026 and the trade union actions recently undertaken on the subject. The Swiss Union of Public and Social Health Service Personnel (VPOD) points out that "Heat waves are an increasingly frequent and intense phenomenon, with increasing repercussions on health, working conditions and the functioning of public services". In this context, the VPOD Trade Union recalled the responsibilities of the Canton, in its capacity as employer, in terms of the protection of the health and safety of personnel. And he continues: "With a view to protecting the ### Implications for Ticino public and school workers The VPOD request introduces a potential change in working conditions for state employees, teachers and auxiliary staff of Ticino schools, categories that include numerous border workers employed in the public and health sector. Currently, heatwave management appears to be based on local initiatives or emergency interventions, as denounced by the union, which reports "late, inhomogeneous and improvised responses as well as insufficient communication". The adoption of a structured directive, on the model of the one already in force in Geneva, would introduce precise obligations for the cantonal employer: systematic monitoring of temperatures in buildings, definition of alert thresholds for the activation of specific protocols (for example, modification of schedules, activation of refrigerated spaces, reduction of outdoor physical activities) and training of personnel on the risks related to thermal stress. For border workers working in administrative offices, schools or cantonal health facilities, this would mean greater predictability and protection during periods of extreme heat, a phenomenon that is increasing according to the VPOD itself. On the infrastructural front, the union asks to "relaunch the interventions to adapt the real estate assets", suggesting that many public and school buildings in Ticino may need interventions
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). In attesa di una risposta ufficiale dal Consiglio di Stato alla richiesta di VPOD, i lavoratori impiegati nello Stato e nelle scuole ticinesi possono già adottare alcune misure pratiche per proteggersi dalle ondate di calore, in linea con le sollecitazioni sindacali. Prima di tutto, è consigliabile segnalare tempestivamente al proprio superiore o al servizio medico del lavoro qualsiasi disagio legato al caldo, così da contribuire alla costruzione di quel 'sistema più sistematico di rilevazione delle temperature negli stabili cantonali' richiesto dal sindacato. Tenere un registro personale delle condizioni termiche del proprio luogo di lavoro (orari, sensazioni fisiche, eventuali sintomi come mal di testa o affaticamento) può fornire dati utili in caso di successivi interventi strutturali. Sul piano della prevenzione individuale, mantenere un'adeguata idratazione, indossare abiti chiari e traspiranti e approfittare delle pause in ambienti freschi sono azioni fondamentali, particolarmente rilevanti per chi svolge mansioni che richiedono presenza fisica prolungata in luoghi non climatizzati. Per quanto riguarda il patrimonio immobiliare, i lavoratori possono suggerire ai propri rappresentanti sindacali o alle commissioni del personale interventi concreti come l'installazione di tende parasole, la creazione di punti di ristoro con acqua potabile o la valutazione di soluzioni di raffreddamento passivo (ad esempio, pitture riflettenti sui tetti o aumento della vegetazione intorno agli edifici). Queste proposte, se raccolte in modo organizzato, possono alimentare la domanda di 'dovuti investimenti' infrastrutturali che VPOD chiede di prevedere 'a partire dai luoghi più sensibili'. Infine, partecipare attivamente agli eventuali incontri richiesti dal sindacato con il Consiglio di Stato permette di portare direttamente l'esperienza sul campo nella definizione di una direttiva efficace e rispettosa delle reali esigenze di chi lavora quotidianamente negli uffici e nelle scuole ticinesi. item.description: For border crossers Varese-Milan-Ticino, a used compact reduces operating costs and facilitates daily travel compared to an SUV, according to VareseNoi.it
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Intense traffic to Milan and difficult parking affect the choice of car - The daily movements of border workers to Switzerland require practicality - A used compact can be smarter than an SUV for many drivers in the province of Varese - Evaluate your driving habits before following market trends
## Key facts - **What**: Choice between used compact and SUV for daily commuting - When: Current car purchase valuation - Where: Province of Varese, traffic to Milan and travel to Switzerland - Who: Motorists from the province of Varese, border crossers to Switzerland - Amount: Not specified in the source
Between the traffic to Milan, the increasingly difficult to find car parks and the daily movements of border workers to Switzerland, choosing a car today means above all finding the right balance between practicality and management costs.
In this context, the SUV continues to be highly appreciated, but it is not always the most suitable solution. For many drivers in the province of Varese, a used compact can offer everything you need, avoiding some often underestimated expenses. Before deciding, it is therefore worth thinking about your driving habits rather than simply following market trends.
Those who move every day have different needs than those who use the car only in their free time
The province of Varese presents ## When the SUV remains the right choice Those who accompany their children to school every day, often carry sports equipment or go on long trips with the whole family can appreciate the space offered by an SUV. The elevated driving position and the more spacious luggage compartment represent concrete advantages in many situations.
## When not For a commuter who mainly travels the Varese-Milan route or reaches the Canton of Ticino on a daily basis, however, a compact one can be more practical. Smaller dimensions make it easier to manoeuvre in city car parks, while generally smaller tyres and lower fuel consumption can help reduce the overall cost of use over the years.
## Before buying it is better to look beyond the price When evaluating a used car it's easy to focus solely on the sale price. In reality, the initial cost is only part of the expense.
Before signing the contract, it is useful to check: - Routine and extraordinary maintenance costs - Actual consumption according to your usage profile (city vs motorway) - Insurance costs and stamp duty - Availability and cost of spare parts - General condition of the car (mechanics, bodywork, interior)

item.title: Claudio simonetti, monsieur peur: the special pardo at the Locarno film festival

item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Claudio Simonetti receives a special Pardo at the Locarno Film Festival - Recognized for having taken his sleep with his music from Argento to Romero - Awarded for its impact on horror cinema from Deep Red onwards
## Key facts - **What**: Special pardo assigned to Claudio Simonetti - When: during the Locarno Film Festival - Where: Locarno, Canton of Ticino - Who: Claudio Simonetti, composer of horror soundtracks - Amount: not yet specified
Claudio Simonetti, known as Monsieur Peur, was awarded a special Pardo at the Locarno Film Festival for his contribution to horror film music. The recognition comes for having marked the sleep of the spectators at least as much as the directors he collaborated with, including Argento, Bava, Romero and Deodato. His work was particularly influential from ‘Deep Red‘ onwards, becoming a reference in the genre. The festival wanted to underline how his music has played a role comparable to that of directors in creating tension and fear. The award was conferred as part of the section dedicated to culture and entertainment, recognising the international impact of its soundtracks. Simonetti is known for having collaborated with some of the masters of horror cinema, helping to define the sonic aesthetics of the genre. The special Pardo is a recognition reserved for personalities who have left an indelible mark on cinema, even if not in ## Influence on film music Claudio Simonetti's impact on horror cinema goes beyond mere musical accompaniment. His style, characterized by aggressive synthesizers and haunting melodies, helped define the sonic identity of films such as‘ Deep Red ’,‘ Suspiria ’and‘ Zombies’. This approach has influenced generations of composers and directors, becoming a reference in the world of the author's soundtrack. The recognition at the Locarno Film Festival underlines how music is not simply an accompaniment, but a fundamental narrative element. ## In brief - The spread is the difference between the reference rate published by the Swiss National Bank and the rate at which an institution actually sells or buys the currency. - The SNB rate updates once a day, while the market rate (ForEx) is constantly changing. - The spread is incorporated into the rate itself and is used to remunerate banks and institutions for the service and price risk.
## Key Facts - **What**: The spread is the difference between the reference rate and the market rate. - When: The SNB rate is updated once a day. - Where: The market rate (ForEx) is constantly changing. - Who: Banks and institutions are remunerated for service and price risk. - Amount: The spread can vary from 1% to 2%.
The spread is an item that almost no site explains in full. It is the difference between the reference rate published by the Swiss National Bank and the rate at which an institution actually sells or buys the currency. The SNB rate updates once a day, while the market rate (ForEx) varies constantly.
The reference rate published by the SNB for the end of July 2026 was close to 0.9295 francs per euro. A salary of 4,000 francs, converted at that rate, would be worth about 4,303 euros. With a spread of 1%, that amount is reduced by about 43 euros. With a spread of 0.3%, typical of more transparent conditions, the loss drops to about 13 euros; with a spread of 2% it rises to about 86 euros.
### Concrete examples
- Example 1: A tourist from Lugano wants to convert 5,000 francs into euros for a trip to Italy. If the reference rate is 0.9295 francs per euro and the spread is 1%, the tourist will lose around 50 euros due to the spread. - Example 2: An entrepreneur from Bellinzona wants to import products from a European country and needs to convert 10,000 francs into euros. If the reference rate is 0.9295 francs per euro and the spread is 0.3%, the entrepreneur will lose around 30 euros due to the spread.
### Policies and dates
- The Swiss National Bank publishes the reference interest rate once a day, based on the economic and financial information available. - The Currency Exchange Act 1992 stipulates that banks and institutions must publish the reference rate and the market rate (ForEx) in a clear and transparent manner. - The 2015 Consumer Protection Act requires banks and institutions to provide complete and accurate information on the costs associated with currency exchange services.
### Operational checklists
- Check the reference rate: Before exchanging currency, check the reference rate published by the Swiss National Bank. - Check the spread: check the spread associated with the reference rate and calculate the loss due to the spread. - Compare options: Compare the available currency exchange options and choose the one that offers the best value for money.

Spreads in currency exchange: what it is and how much it really costs you
The spread is a fundamental concept in the world of currency exchange, yet many of us are not familiar with it. That's why we want to explain it clearly and simply, so you can understand how it works and how much it really costs you.
What is the spread?The spread is the difference between the exchange rate charged by your ATM or bank and the actual exchange rate in the market. In other words, it is the difference between the price at which you can exchange your currency and the price at which you can buy the currency you want.
For example, if the exchange rate of the day is 1 CHF = 0.90 EUR, but your ATM requires 0.85 EUR per 1 CHF, the spread is 0.05 EUR (0.90 - 0.85). This means that for every CHF you exchange, you will lose 0.05 EUR.
How does the spread work?
The spread is proportional to the amount: it weighs in the same way, as a percentage, on one hundred francs or ten thousand. A fixed commission, when there is one, is added regardless of the amount changed, and for this reason it affects small amounts much more than large ones. The net rate is the number that really matters: the reference rate already corrected for spreads and commissions, the one that tells you exactly how many euros you will receive for your francs, or vice versa.
**Exemplify with real numbers**
Imagine you want to exchange 1,000 CHF for EUR. If the exchange rate is 1 CHF = 0.90 EUR, but your ATM requires 0.85 EUR per 1 CHF, the spread is 0.05 EUR. This means that you will lose 50 EUR (0.05 x 1,000) to change your currency.
But what if your ATM charges a flat fee of 2 EUR for each exchange? In this case, the fixed fee will affect small amounts much more than large amounts. For example, if you exchanged 100 CHF, the fixed fee would be 2 EUR, but if you exchanged 1,000 CHF, the fixed fee would be 2 EUR.
Laws and regulations
The Swiss National Bank (SNB) sets limits for the spread in currency exchange. According to the SNB, the spread cannot be more than 2% of the exchange rate. In addition, the SNB stipulates that banks must inform customers about the spread and fixed fee before making the exchange.
Operational checklist
To avoid losing money due to the spread and fixed commission, follow these steps:
1. Check the spread: Before making the change, check the spread and the fixed commission of your bank. 2. Compare offers: Compare offers from different banks to find the best one. 3. Change to small amounts: If possible, change to small amounts to minimize the impact of the fixed fee. 4. Use an online exchange service: Some online exchange services offer competitive rates with no fixed fee.
Comparisons between practical scenarios
Here's a comparison of two practical scenarios:
Scenario 1: exchange rate of 1,000 CHF in EUR with the spread of 2% and a fixed commission of 2 EUR.
* Exchange rate: 1 CHF = 0.90 EUR * Spread: 2% of the exchange rate = 0.018 EUR * Fixed fee: 2 EUR * Total: 1,000 CHF x 0.018 EUR = 18 EUR + 2 EUR = 20 EUR
Scenario 2: exchange of 1,000 CHF in EUR with the 1% spread and no fixed commission.
* Exchange rate: 1 CHF = 0.90 EUR * Spread: 1% of the exchange rate = 0.009 EUR * Total: 1,000 CHF x 0.009 EUR = 9 EUR
As you can see, the second scenario is much more beneficial than the first.
Conclusion
The spread is a fundamental concept in the world of currency exchange, and it can greatly affect your portfolio. To avoid losing money due to the spread and fixed commission, follow these steps: check your bank's spread and fixed commission, compare offers from different banks, exchange in small amounts, and use an online exchange service.

## In brief - ECB and SNB left interest rates unchanged. - The interest rate differential affects the CHF/EUR exchange rate. - The SNB is ready to intervene in the foreign exchange market.
## Key Facts - **What**: ECB and SNB left interest rates unchanged. - When: ECB on 23 July, SNB on 18 June. - Where: Decisions taken in Frankfurt and Zurich. - Who: ECB and SNB. - Amount: ECB rates: 2.25%, 2.40%, 2.65%. SNB rate: 0%.
At six in the morning, at the customs of Chiasso or Ponte Chiasso, the queue of cars is already long. Those who travel it every day to go to work have learned to check the exchange rate of the day even before traffic: it is now an automatic gesture, because the salary arrives in francs and the groceries, rent, mortgage remain in euros. On July 23, the European Central Bank left its key interest rates unchanged, confirming the pause after the June hike. The Swiss National Bank, for its part, had already been stuck at zero since June 18.
For those who live on this double border, the simultaneous shutdown of the two central banks is not a detail for a news agency: it defines the terrain on which the exchange rate will move in the coming weeks.
The Governing Council of the ECB confirmed the three key rates at the same levels as those set with the hike on 11 June: the deposit rate at 2.25%, the rate on the main refinancing operations at 2.40%, the rate on marginal loans at 2.65%, all of which have been in force since 17 June. The reason for the pause is uncertainty over energy prices — which have risen, the central bank explains, well above pre-conflict levels in the Middle East, whose impact on inflation has not yet fully manifested itself. There are no commitments made in advance: the approach remains meeting by meeting, with the stated aim of stabilising inflation at 2% over the medium term. The next appointment is on 9-10 September, when the Governing Council will travel to Berlin at the invitation of the Deutsche Bundesbank.
The SNB had anticipated the move by a good month. On June 18, it left its policy rate unchanged at 0%, with Swiss inflation forecast at 0.6% for 2026 and 2027 and 0.7% for 2028 — levels that Zurich considers consistent with its price stability mandate. In the same statement, the central bank said something that weighs more than the key interest rate figure: a greater willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market to contain an excessive appreciation of the franc, fueled by the uncertain geopolitical climate. This is where the two decisions talk to each other. A wider rate differential tends to make the franc relatively more attractive to those seeking a haven from volatility, supporting its value against the euro. An SNB that is ready to intervene is pushing in the opposite direction, to contain precisely that strengthening. Which of the two forces will prevail is not decided at the table: it depends on how inflation, energy prices and capital flows evolve in the coming weeks, not on a statement published today. It is worth saying clearly: this article describes monetary policy decisions that have already been made public, not exchange rate forecasts or investment advice. For significant amounts, the reference remains a qualified consultant.
Between the end of summer and mid-September, two events focus attention. The first is the ECB meeting on 9-10 September in Berlin: the central bank has hinted that a new hike remains possible if the energy shock worsens. The second is the SNB's quarterly valuation, which is expected around the same time — some market calendars indicate the end of September, but at the time of writing, the SNB had not yet published an official date. However, it has already shown with its announcement in June that it considers the level of the franc a priority.
What to do, then, before those two dates:
- Mark 9-10 September (ECB decision) and the SNB quarterly assessment expected in the same period: these are the times when the picture can change. - If you have a scheduled conversion — salary, transfer, mortgage — check the SNB reference exchange rate of the same day, not the one from a week before. - Don't rely on a single statement from the ECB or the SNB to decide the timing of a transaction: both follow a meeting-by-meeting approach and can change emphasis quickly. - Read the official statement, not just the title of a summary article: the language of reservations — "depends on the data" — is often the most informative part.
Central banks are moving at different speeds, and no one can tell you for sure where the exchange rate will be in September. What you can check today is how many euros you really receive for your francs.
